descripcion_es: Actions that started in the past and are still going on or have just finished; duration with for and since.
resumen: It is formed with have/has been + -ing verb. It is used to talk about an activity that started in the past and continues now (or has just finished), with the emphasis on duration.

filas: She has been working here for two years.
I haven't been sleeping well lately.
How long have you been waiting?

explicacion.texto: It often corresponds to Spanish “llevar + gerundio” or “hace … que”: “Llevo una hora esperando” = I have been waiting for an hour. In English the present simple is NOT used for this.

filas: for ten minutes, for three years, for ages

items: Duration of something that is still going on: It has been raining all day.
Recent activity with a visible result: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?
How long asks about duration: How long have they been living in Madrid?

explicacion.texto: Continuous versus simple: the continuous focuses on the activity and its duration (I've been reading this book all week); the simple focuses on the result or the finished quantity (I've read three chapters). With state verbs (know, like, want, believe, own) we use the simple: I've known her for years, not I've been knowing.

ejemplos.frase: We have been living in this flat since March.
ejemplos.traduccion: Vivimos en este piso desde marzo.

ejemplos.frase: How long have you been learning English?
I'm tired because I've been running.
ejemplos.traduccion: Estoy cansado porque he estado corriendo.

ejemplos.frase: It has been snowing for three days.
She hasn't been feeling well recently.
They've been arguing about money for weeks.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I am waiting for you since five o'clock.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I have been waiting for you since five o'clock.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “llevo esperando desde…” is not translated with the present continuous but with the present perfect continuous.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I've been knowing him for ten years.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I've known him for ten years.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Know is a state verb: it has no continuous form.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: She has been working here since two years.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: She has been working here for two years.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a period of time we use for; since goes with the starting point.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the present perfect continuous.
ejercicios.frase: I ___ (wait) for the bus for twenty minutes.
ejercicios.explicacion: The affirmative form from the table applies: have/has been + -ing. The clue is for twenty minutes, which measures the length of a wait that started in the past and is still going on. With the subject I we use have, which can be contracted: I have been waiting or I've been waiting. It is exactly the case of Spanish “llevar + gerundio”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: An action that started in the past and continues: have been + -ing.
ejercicios.traduccion: Llevo veinte minutos esperando el autobús.

errores_previstos.respuesta: am waiting
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the Spanish present (“espero desde hace”): with for and an action lasting until now, English uses have been waiting.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have been wait
errores_previstos.explicacion: After been the verb takes -ing: have been waiting.

errores_previstos.respuesta: has been waiting
errores_previstos.explicacion: With I the auxiliary is have; has is only for the third person singular.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the present perfect continuous.
ejercicios.frase: She ___ (study) French since she was twelve.
ejercicios.explicacion: The affirmative form from the table applies, with a third-person subject: has been + -ing. The clue is since she was twelve, which marks the starting point of an activity that continues in the present. So it is she has been studying (or she's been studying). Note that Spanish uses the present here (“estudia desde…”), but English needs the present perfect continuous.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estudia francés desde los doce años.

errores_previstos.respuesta: studies
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the Spanish present: with since and an activity that continues we use has been studying.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have been studying
errores_previstos.explicacion: With she the auxiliary is has, not have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: is studying
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present continuous is not combined with since to express duration up to now: has been studying.

ejercicios.frase: They have been playing tennis ___ two hours.
ejercicios.explicacion: The for and since table applies: for goes with a duration and since with a starting point. The clue is two hours, which is an amount of time, not a clock time or a date. That's why it takes for. A simple test: if you can answer “how long?”, it is for; if you answer “since when?”, it is since.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Two hours is a duration, so for.
ejercicios.traduccion: Llevan dos horas jugando al tenis.

errores_previstos.respuesta: since
errores_previstos.explicacion: Since needs a starting point (since 3 o'clock); two hours is a duration and needs for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: during
errores_previstos.explicacion: During means “in the course of” a specific period (during the match); for duration up to now we use for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: from
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “desde hace”: from needs a to or a starting point, not a duration.

ejercicios.frase: It has been raining ___ last night.
ejercicios.explicacion: The for and since table applies. The clue is last night, which is a specific moment when the rain started, not an amount of time; that's why it takes since. The full sentence uses the form from the unit for the duration of something still going on: It has been raining since last night. Remember that with last no other word goes in front (not “since the last night”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Last night is the starting point, so since.

errores_previstos.respuesta: for
errores_previstos.explicacion: For goes with durations (for two hours); last night is the starting point and needs since.

errores_previstos.respuesta: from
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “desde”: from is used with from… to…; for the start of something still going on, since.

errores_previstos.respuesta: since the
errores_previstos.explicacion: With last there is no article: since last night.

ejercicios.explicacion: The question structure from the table applies, have/has + subject + been + -ing, together with the note that how long asks about duration. The clue is How long, which asks about a time that lasts until now. So it is have you been working. Spanish says “¿cuánto llevas trabajando?”, with no perfect tense, which encourages you to use the present; in English that is a mistake.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: How long + an action that continues needs the present perfect continuous.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas trabajando para esta empresa?

por_opcion.are you working: Incorrect: the present continuous does not express duration up to now; how long are you working would at most ask about a future plan.
por_opcion.have you been working: Correct: how long + have + subject + been + -ing for an activity that started in the past and continues.
por_opcion.do you work: Incorrect: the present simple with how long is a calque of Spanish; it does not express duration up to the present moment.

ejercicios.frase: I ___ Laura since we were at school.
ejercicios.explicacion: The note in the unit applies: with state verbs (know, like, want, believe, own) we use the present perfect simple, not the continuous form. The clue is the verb know, which describes a state, not an activity, together with since, which needs the present perfect. So it is have known, although in Spanish we use the present “conozco”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Know is a state verb and is not used in the continuous form.
ejercicios.traduccion: Conozco a Laura desde que íbamos al colegio.

por_opcion.have known: Correct: present perfect simple, because know is a state verb with no continuous form.
por_opcion.have been knowing: Incorrect: know is a state verb and is not used in the continuous form.
por_opcion.know: Incorrect: a calque of the Spanish present; with since for something lasting until now you need the present perfect.

ejercicios.explicacion: The note in the unit about a recent activity with a visible result applies: we use the continuous form to ask about the activity that explains what we can see now. The clue is Your hands are dirty: dirty hands are the result of something the person has been doing until a moment ago. So it is What have you been doing?, which asks about the activity, not about a finished result.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A recent activity with a visible result: continuous form.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tienes las manos sucias. ¿Qué has estado haciendo?

por_opcion.have you done: Incorrect here: the present perfect simple asks about something finished or its result (What have you done? sounds almost like a reproach for some mischief). What explains the dirty hands is the activity.
por_opcion.have you been doing: Correct: continuous form for a recent activity with a visible result.
por_opcion.did you do: Incorrect: the past simple places the action at a finished moment in the past, and here the activity is connected to the present.

ejercicios.explicacion: The note in the unit on continuous versus simple applies: the continuous focuses on the activity and its duration, while the simple focuses on the result or the finished quantity. The clue is three emails, a specific number of finished things. So it takes the present perfect simple, I've written. With the continuous form you would say I've been writing emails all morning, with no quantity.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A finished quantity is given (three emails): present perfect simple.
ejercicios.traduccion: He escrito tres correos esta mañana.

por_opcion.written: Correct: present perfect simple (I've written) for a finished quantity.
por_opcion.been writing: Incorrect: the continuous form is not combined with a specific number of finished things; you would say I've been writing emails all morning.
por_opcion.write: Incorrect: after have you need the past participle (written), not the infinitive.

respuestas: We have been living here since 2018.
ejercicios.explicacion: The note in the unit applies: English does not use the present to express something that started in the past and continues. The clue is since 2018, a past starting point of a situation that continues. The expected correction is We have been living here since 2018. The present perfect simple is also accepted (We have lived here since 2018), because with live, work or study both are correct and almost interchangeable; the continuous puts slightly more emphasis on duration or on the situation being temporary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With since for something that continues we use have been + -ing (or the present perfect simple, have lived), not the present continuous.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We are living here since 2018.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is the uncorrected sentence: the present continuous cannot go with since to express duration up to now.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We live here since 2018.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the Spanish present (“vivimos aquí desde”): with since you need the present perfect.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We have been living here for 2018.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The tense is right, but 2018 is a starting point and needs since, not for.

ejercicios.frase: He has been driving since three hours.
respuestas: He has been driving for three hours.
He's been driving for three hours.
ejercicios.explicacion: The for and since table applies. The tense is already correct (has been driving); the mistake is in the preposition. The clue is three hours, a duration, not a starting point, so it takes for. Since three hours is a calque of Spanish “desde hace tres horas”, which mixes the two ideas.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Three hours is a duration: for, not since.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He has been driving since three hours.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is the uncorrected sentence: with a duration we use for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He has been driving during three hours.
errores_previstos.explicacion: During does not express duration up to now; we use for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He is driving for three hours.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The preposition has been fixed but the tense has been broken: you need has been driving.

ejercicios.enunciado: Turn it into a question with How long.
ejercicios.frase: You have been learning the piano.
respuestas: How long have you been learning the piano?
ejercicios.explicacion: The question structure from the table applies: how long + have/has + subject + been + -ing. The clue is the instruction to ask about duration, which in English is always done with how long. To form the question, swap the auxiliary have and the subject you, and been learning stays after them: How long have you been learning the piano?
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas aprendiendo a tocar el piano?

errores_previstos.respuesta: How long you have been learning the piano?
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the question the auxiliary have goes before the subject: have you.

errores_previstos.respuesta: How long are you learning the piano?
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the present: for duration up to now you need have you been learning.

errores_previstos.respuesta: How long have you been learn the piano?
errores_previstos.explicacion: After been the verb takes -ing: learning.

respuestas: She has not been sleeping well.
ejercicios.explicacion: The negative form from the table applies: haven't/hasn't been + -ing. The clue is the subject she, third person, whose auxiliary is has. The negative goes right after has, not after been: She hasn't been sleeping well, or uncontracted, She has not been sleeping well. Been and sleeping do not change.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The negative goes with has: hasn't been + -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She has been not sleeping well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The negative goes with the auxiliary has: hasn't been, not been not.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She doesn't have been sleeping well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present perfect does not use do; the negative is formed with has not.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She haven't been sleeping well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With she the auxiliary is has: hasn't.

respuestas: they have been talking for ages
ejercicios.explicacion: The affirmative word order applies: subject + have been + -ing + for + duration. The clue is the word for, which must go before the duration ages; for ages is an informal expression meaning “a very long time”. So it is they have been talking for ages: auxiliary, been and -ing verb together, with nothing in between.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they have been for ages talking
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the Spanish order “llevan siglos hablando”: the time expression goes at the end, after the verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they been have talking for ages
errores_previstos.explicacion: The auxiliary order is fixed: have + been + -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they have talking been for ages
errores_previstos.explicacion: Been always goes before the -ing verb: have been talking.

respuestas: how long have you been waiting
ejercicios.explicacion: The question structure from the unit applies: how long + have + subject + been + -ing. The clue is the word how, which together with long forms the question phrase for duration and goes at the beginning. Then comes the auxiliary have, then the subject you, and finally been waiting. It is one of the most useful questions in this unit.

errores_previstos.respuesta: how long you have been waiting
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the question the auxiliary have goes before the subject: have you.

errores_previstos.respuesta: how long have been you waiting
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject goes right after have, not after been.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have you been waiting how long
errores_previstos.explicacion: The question phrase how long goes at the beginning of the question.

descripcion_larga_es: The present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing) expresses an activity that started in the past and continues now, or has just finished, with the emphasis on duration. It often corresponds to Spanish “llevar + gerundio” or “hace… que”. Spanish speakers find it difficult because they tend to use the present (“I am waiting since…”), to confuse for and since and to use the continuous form with state verbs.

contexto.que_es: It is a tense formed with have or has + been + -ing verb. It indicates an activity that began in the past and continues in the present, or that has just finished and left a visible result, and it emphasises its duration. It usually goes with for (duration), since (starting point) or the question how long.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is the natural way of saying how long you have been doing something: working somewhere, studying a language, waiting for someone. Using the present simple or continuous instead (“I work here since 2020”) is one of the most typical mistakes of Spanish speakers and sounds very strange to a native speaker. In an interview or an oral exam it comes up as soon as you talk about your background.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When you say or ask how long something that is still happening has lasted (How long have you been learning English?) or explain a visible result of a recent activity (Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?). The signals are for, since, how long, all day, lately. Where Spanish says “llevo dos años estudiando” or “estudio desde 2020”, English uses have been studying.
